text: The vague fear of lock-in that Lesson 5 named as a bad reason to go multi-cloud has a second, inward-facing version: building elaborate custom abstraction layers over every cloud service, just in case the organization ever needs to switch providers, even when nobody has named a specific trigger. The honest goal isn't eliminating lock-in everywhere. It's knowing exactly where you have it, why, and whether it was a deliberate trade or an accident nobody evaluated.

Some portability is genuinely cheap to adopt, because you'd want the underlying pattern anyway. A containerized workload on Kubernetes behaves close to the same way across AKS, EKS, and GKE, and you were going to containerize it regardless of multi-cloud. Terraform's HCL modules don't run unmodified across providers, but the declarative skill and workflow transfer directly, making a Terraform-fluent team productive on a second provider far faster than starting cold. Open data formats and standard protocols keep a door open the same way, at little extra cost.

Contrast that with the pattern that quietly wastes enormous engineering time: a homegrown wrapper around storage, queuing, or managed databases, built so that, hypothetically, you could swap providers underneath it. It has to be maintained forever by your own team instead of the provider. It rarely covers everything the underlying service does, so teams work around it the moment they need a provider-specific feature. And it slows down every feature built on top of it, permanently, to protect against a switch that, for most organizations, never actually happens.

None of this means lock-in is always bad. A fully-managed database or identity platform that removes real operational burden is often worth the lock-in that comes with it, as long as that trade was made consciously, with the savings documented. The actual failure mode isn't lock-in itself — it's lock-in nobody ever evaluated, sitting next to an abstraction layer nobody needed, both unexamined and both costing the organization at the same time.

The working rule: adopt a portable pattern when you'd want it anyway for reasons unrelated to multi-cloud, accept a proprietary service deliberately when its savings are real, and build a custom abstraction layer only when a specific, named migration is already planned. With the strategy decided, Chapter 3 turns to the mechanics — starting with exactly how far Kubernetes portability really extends, and where it quietly stops.
